title: FDA Advisers Vote to Ease Restrictions on Popular Peptides Like BPC-157
excerpt: An FDA advisory panel backed broader pharmacy access for four peptides in narrow votes, overriding agency scientists' concerns about limited clinical evidence.
body:
• An FDA advisory panel voted 8-6 to recommend adding peptides BPC-157, KPV and TB-500 to a list allowing pharmacy compounding; MOTS-C passed 7-5.
  • The votes override FDA staff scientists who advised against the move, citing scant clinical evidence for the peptides' safety and effectiveness.
  • Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has championed the push; critics say many panelists who voted yes have financial ties to the peptide industry.
  • The FDA is not bound by the panel's recommendations and will make a final decision; three more peptides face votes on Friday.

Panel Backs Four Peptides in Narrow Votes

A majority of the U.S. Food and Drug Administration's outside advisers voted on Thursday to support allowing pharmacies to compound four popular peptides, advancing a deregulatory push championed by Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

https://x.com/HISteveWilliams/status/2080421389660733472

The FDA's Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee voted 8-6, with one abstention, to recommend adding BPC-157, KPV and TB-500 to Category 1 of the agency's 503A bulks list — the regulatory designation that permits compounding pharmacies to prepare customised treatments for patients with a prescription. MOTS-C, being evaluated for obesity and osteoporosis, passed 7-5 with two abstentions, according to Reuters.

The two-day meeting pits FDA career scientists — who released a report last month advising against the move — against a telehealth industry eager to tap what analysts estimate could quickly become a $2 billion to $3 billion market.

A Boom Built on Anecdotal Evidence

Peptides are drugs built from short chains of amino acids, the same building blocks the body uses to make proteins. Injectable versions of BPC-157, TB-500 and others are already sold widely online for everything from muscle recovery to longevity through a gray market that exploits the allowable use of unapproved medicines for research purposes. The combination of BPC-157 and TB-500 is popularly known as the "Wolverine stack" for its purported injury-healing properties.

The Biden administration in 2023 restricted compounding of nearly 20 peptides over safety concerns. In April, Kennedy reclassified 12 of them as Category 1 substances, the first regulatory step toward restoring pharmacy access. A survey of 500 doctors conducted by Sermo found that 48% had patients disclose using a non-FDA-approved peptide in the past year, according to MarketWatch.

"The substance's supposed benefits are largely based on anecdotal evidence, and the interest in it appears to be driven by those who stand to benefit from increased demand."

— Nina Zeldes, Public Citizen's Health Research Group

FDA official Matt Lash told the committee that compounded products are not required to carry labels notifying patients of safety information or dosing. Russell Wesdyk, another agency official, encouraged the industry to pursue investigational new drug applications and conduct human clinical trials.

Conflicts of Interest Under Scrutiny

The advisory panel's composition has drawn sharp criticism. The 14-member committee added seven people who operate or work for clinics and businesses selling peptide treatments prior to the meeting. Many members who voted in favour could stand to gain commercially from broader peptide access.

"How is that acceptable?" asked Paul Knoepfler, a professor of cell biology at UC Davis, according to Reuters.

HHS spokesperson Emily Hilliard defended the process, saying all committee members underwent the same ethics review required of FDA advisory committee members. Those who voted against the peptides were largely doctors and patient representatives.

"I'm concerned that we're responding to a market-induced demand rather than a decision based in solid science."

— Elizabeth Rebello, University of Texas, panel member

Market Implications and the Telehealth Race

Shares of Hims & Hers Health surged as much as 12% during Thursday's session before closing 3.3% higher at $32.74. The telehealth company, which acquired a peptide manufacturing facility last year, had its chief medical officer Anant Vinjamoori testify before the panel in favour of regulated access.

Leerink Partners analyst Michael Cherny estimated the peptide compounding market at $2.2 billion, while Needham & Co pegged it at $3.3 billion.

For Indian-American physicians — a substantial segment of the U.S. medical workforce — the regulatory shift raises practical questions about prescribing compounds that lack robust clinical validation. The debate also resonates with India's pharmaceutical industry, where peptide synthesis is a growing export segment.

What Happens Next

The committee reconvenes on Friday to vote on three remaining peptides: emideltide, epitalon and Semax. The FDA is not bound by its advisory panel's recommendations and will make the final determination on whether to allow compounding.

Even if the agency agrees, compounded peptides would not be FDA-approved products — a distinction that carries significant weight. A former FDA official told Reuters that rulemaking could take up to a year. Nearly no other country has approved the use of these peptides; only Semax has formal regulatory clearance, in Russia.

Consumer-safety advocates warn that legitimising compounds with thin evidence bases sets a troubling precedent. Adriane Fugh-Berman, director of Georgetown University Medical Center's PharmedOut programme, told the committee that "peptides prepared to the highest standards are still untested experimental drugs."
nri_angle: The regulatory shift raises questions for Indian-American physicians about prescribing unvalidated compounds and resonates with India's growing peptide synthesis export sector.
